entries.title: The moonshine still in Eden
entries.question: Did your family ever tell Prohibition stories about the Valley?
body: At 4 o’clock on a Sunday morning, Oct. 17, 1926, Weber County Sheriff Richard Pincock and his deputies crept up on a dugout near Eden “just as dawn was breaking.” They had found it earlier but waited, afraid the men inside might escape in the dark.

Inside the 40-by-28-foot dugout was what the Ogden Standard-Examiner called “one of the largest moonshine distilling plants discovered in Weber county for many months.” The still was “going full blast,” with a stream of whiskey “as large as a lead pencil” pouring from it.

Officers seized a 100-gallon still, 2,100 gallons of mash in 50-gallon barrels, 1,600 pounds of sugar and 80 gallons of whiskey in five-gallon kegs. One man was washing his hands at the creek; the other was asleep on a pile of straw. Both were arrested and released on bond. The farmer who owned the land said he had leased the patch and didn’t know what it was being used for.
The next day the paper ran a staff photo of the still. The sheriff is holding a small flag the paper said the distillers used for a “wig-wag” signaling system.

entries.title: Opening day of the 1926 deer hunt
entries.question: What’s changed most since 1926: the rules, the gear, or the deer?
body: Utah’s deer hunt opened Oct. 20, 1926, and several Ogden hunting parties headed for the mountains days early. The rules, as printed in the Standard-Examiner:

• Bucks only, with horns at least six inches long. • Hunters had to be over 16, with a red cap and a hunting license. • One buck per hunter, “providing he can shoot or run him down.” • The season ran just 10 days, ending the evening of Oct. 30.
The game warden reminded hunters to stay off game preserves, respect farmers’ land, not shoot cattle, and “preserve human life.” Fishing at Strawberry Reservoir and Fish Lake closed the same day.

entries.title: A benefit dance in Huntsville
entries.question: What’s a time your neighbors came through for someone?
body: On Friday, Oct. 22, 1926, Huntsville held a benefit dance at the ward social hall at 8 p.m. The Modern Woodmen lodge put it on, Spillman’s orchestra came up from Ogden, and the money went to help an Ogden Valley farmer who had been sick for a long time.
“The public is invited to attend.” A hundred years later, the Valley still shows up for its own.

entries.title: A week in Huntsville
entries.question: Is your family in the old Huntsville news? What traditions has your family kept going?
body: The Huntsville news in the Standard-Examiner, October 1926: the Daughters of the Pioneers started their winter meetings in a member’s home; Sunday sacrament meeting moved to the afternoon and the winter course of the Mutuals began; a group of couples made a temple trip to Salt Lake; and the Relief Society bazaar was “very successful.”
Look closely at the clipping: the names of the families are right there.

entries.title: The great leaf question
entries.question: How do you handle leaves now?
body: 1926: “What to do with ’em?” Ogden had banned burning leaves after Sept. 1, for safety and to stop “the smoke nuisance,” and leaves weren’t allowed in the gutters because they clogged the storm sewers. The city had no money to haul them, so residents and commissioners alike were asking what to do. The paper even ran a three-panel cartoon: rake the leaves after a hard day at the office, pile them up neatly, and watch the wind blow them all over the yard again.
1962: Ogden had an answer: a vacuum truck for leaves only. The street superintendent warned residents not to include any other rubbish.

entries.title: Fire at the Ogden Canyon Sanitarium
entries.question: Did your family ever visit the old canyon resorts?
body: Early on Oct. 23, 1926, the Ogden Canyon Sanitarium burned, the third time fire had destroyed the resort. Fanned by a brisk mountain wind, it was soon in ruins; by morning only bare brick walls stood among the charred timbers.
The paper said the fire likely started from an overheated stove in the women’s dressing room on the north side of the building.

entries.title: What's under Pineview? Artesian Park
entries.question: Did your family ever talk about the wells or picnicking out there before the dam?
entries.source: Ogden Standard-Examiner, July 8, 1920 (photo: Fred Pack, about 1920, J. Willard Marriott Library, University of Utah)
body: About 1920, this was “Artesian Park” near Huntsville. Water bubbled up out of the ground on its own. Photographer Fred Pack saw what the area could do, and Ogden City drilled these artesian wells in 1915. The spot later became a favorite picnic place.

On July 7, 1920, Mayor Frank Francis and the city commissioners took a trip up to the wells. The engineers with them agreed that with a pumping plant, “an almost unlimited supply of water” could come from the wells, and they said the water came from a gravel bed, so there was “no danger of the wells becoming closed.”
Today it’s all under Pineview Reservoir.
Kids can ride the Time Train to watch the wells turn into Pineview, one stop at a time.

entries.ago: More than 100 years ago, and this week
entries.title: Beneath Pineview: When Low Water Shows Us the Old Valley
entries.question: Have you walked out on the lakebed this fall? Did you spot anything that's usually underwater?
entries.source: Ogden City Records Office photographs (1914 and 1915); Utah Humanities; Weber State University. Photo: Shauna Miller, Pineview, October 2026
entries.alt: Two yellow cottonwoods frame Pineview's dry lakebed and the mountains, seen from the trail, October 2026, photo by Shauna Miller
body: Photographs kept by the Ogden City Records Office for more than a century show the artesian wells being drilled near Huntsville in 1914 and 1915. By accident they also show something else: Ogden Valley about 20 years before Pineview Dam was built.

Whoever took them wrote notes right on the prints. One, dated Nov. 17, 1914, reads “Wells at Huntsville, Well #7, Flow 530 g.p.m.” Four men stand around the well while a column of water bursts out of the ground. That’s 530 gallons a minute, with no pump.
Another photo from the same day is labeled Well #8, with a 4-inch pipe and “Down 80'.” Instead of a finished well, it shows the drilling rig standing in an open field with the mountains behind it.

The wide shot of several flowing wells may be the most striking. Water pours from the pipes across the field, with trees, farm buildings and fields stretching into the distance. Look past the wells for a minute. This is land we now think of as lake and shoreline, back when it was still open country.

The wells were soon tied together into one system. A photo labeled “Setting Valves for Intake at City Wells, Aug. & Sept. 1915” shows a row of valves pouring water into a concrete collection basin. When the remains of structures like this show up in the mud at Pineview today, they can look strange. A century ago, they were a carefully built way to collect and control the water.

The area became known as Artesian Park. Drilling started in 1914, and about 51 wells were drilled over the years that followed. Work on Pineview Dam began in 1934, and when the dam was finished in 1937, the reservoir covered Artesian Park under 30 to 40 feet of water. Because the wells were capped below the clay, they kept supplying Ogden even underwater. Roads fell out of use, buildings were moved, and the old waterworks disappeared from view.

That’s why these old photos matter now. With Pineview this low, concrete, pipes, old roads and foundations are coming back into view after decades underwater. Without photos and records like these, some of it would just be unexplained concrete sticking out of the mud.

This week, from the trail along the shore, the lakebed stretches almost all the way to the mountains. From up there you can see how much ground the water has given back, but you can’t tell what any of it used to be. For that, we still need the photographs, maps and records kept by places like the Ogden City Records Office.

The old photos show us what was there. The new ones show us what’s left. Together they remind us that Pineview didn’t erase the old Ogden Valley. It covered it. Every so often, when the water drops far enough, the old valley gets to show itself again.
Find more in the Ogden City Records Office’s “Beneath Pineview” story map.
